No direct Messianic link is drawn for the units themselves; they are the honest background against which his teaching about wealth and worship is heard.

Topic: Messiah ben David and Messiah ben Joseph
Summary: Rabbinic tradition speaks of two messianic figures: Messiah ben David, the victorious king from David's line, and Messiah ben Joseph, a suffering messiah who is slain in battle before the final redemption.
JewishBackground: The two-messiah idea appears in rabbinic literature, most famously in the Babylonian Talmud (Sukkah 52a), where Zechariah 12:10 is read of mourning for Messiah ben Joseph who was slain. Messiah ben Joseph, from the tribe of Joseph, was understood to fight the wars of God and fall, after which Messiah ben David would come in victory and restore Israel. The tradition wrestles honestly with a tension in the prophetic texts: some pictures show a conquering king, others a suffering figure. Not all Jewish thinkers held the two-messiah scheme; some read all the promises of one Davidic Messiah. This entry describes the tradition, not a unanimous Jewish doctrine.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that the two pictures belong to one Messiah in two comings: Jesus was slain like the suffering figure and will return as the victorious king. The disciples themselves wrestled with the same tension until the resurrection, when Jesus explained from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer before entering glory (Luke 24:25-27). Where Jewish tradition holds two figures apart, Christians hold one Messiah fulfilling both roles.
RelatedTopics: Messiah; Suffering; Kingdom of God; Hope

Summary: Daniel saw 'one like the Son of man' coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will never pass away.
JewishBackground: In Daniel 7, the Son of Man is a heavenly figure, distinct from the four beasts that represent earthly empires. In Second Temple literature, notably the Parables of Enoch, a Son of Man figure appears as a preexistent heavenly judge. Rabbinic reading varied: some identified the figure with Israel itself, others read it messianically. The title therefore carried both human and heavenly associations in first-century Judaism, which is why it could serve as a claim to more than ordinary humanity.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that Jesus deliberately took this title as his own — it is his most frequent self-designation in the Gospels — and that at his trial he joined Daniel 7 to Psalm 110, telling the high priest they would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power and coming on the clouds (Matthew 26:64). The Christian claim is that the heavenly figure of Daniel's vision is Jesus himself.
RelatedTopics: Messiah; Prophecy; Kingdom of God; Judgment

Summary: 'The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand' — a royal psalm in which David's Lord is also a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
JewishBackground: Psalm 110 is a royal psalm, and Jewish tradition has read it in more than one way: of David himself, of Abraham, or of a coming Davidic king. The Melchizedek priesthood in verse 4 is distinctive, since kingship and priesthood were normally kept apart in Israel. Some ancient Jewish readings are messianic; mainstream rabbinic tradition largely reads the psalm of a past king rather than of the future Messiah. The difference is stated plainly here rather than smoothed over.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading follows Jesus' own argument: when he asked how David could call the Messiah 'Lord' if the Messiah were merely David's son (Matthew 22:41-46), no one could answer him. Hebrews builds the whole priesthood of Christ on this psalm: a priest forever after Melchizedek's order, not Aaron's, seated at God's right hand.

Summary: A shoot from the stump of Jesse, a righteous Branch from David's line — the prophets' image of a king who rises after the royal tree has been cut down.
JewishBackground: Isaiah 11 pictures a shoot growing from Jesse's stump after judgment has felled the tree, and Jeremiah 23 names the coming king 'a righteous Branch.' Zechariah calls God's servant 'the Branch' and pictures him building the Temple. The Targums make the messianic reading explicit in places, rendering the Branch of Isaiah 11 as the Messiah. The image holds judgment and hope together: the old kingdom falls, but the root survives.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that Jesus is the shoot from Jesse's line — Luke traces his genealogy to David and to Jesse — and the righteous Branch who reigns in justice where the old kings failed. The Branch's Temple-building in Zechariah is read of the church, the living temple Christ builds.

Summary: 'There shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel' — Balaam's oracle of a coming ruler, read messianically in Second Temple Judaism.
JewishBackground: Balaam, hired to curse Israel, instead blessed it and spoke of a star and sceptre from Jacob. The Targum of Onkelos renders the verse of a king and a Messiah, and in the second century Simon bar Kokhba took his name — 'son of the star' — from this very verse, showing how firmly it was read as a messianic promise. The oracle's star and sceptre join heavenly sign to royal rule.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that Matthew's star over Bethlehem answers Balaam's star, and that Revelation names Jesus himself 'the bright and morning star.' Where bar Kokhba's star set in defeat, Christians hold that Jesus' star still rises.

Topic: Isaiah 7:14: The Virgin and the Young Woman
Summary: 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel' — a sign given to King Ahaz, read very differently in Jewish and Christian tradition.
JewishBackground: The Hebrew word is 'almah, meaning a young woman of marriageable age; it does not by itself mean 'virgin.' Jewish reading commonly places the sign in Ahaz's own day, often identifying the child with Hezekiah. But the ancient Greek Septuagint, translated by Jewish scholars centuries before Jesus, rendered 'almah as 'parthenos,' meaning virgin — and that Greek text was the Bible of much of the early church. Both facts are stated here, since the debate turns on them.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading follows Matthew, who quotes the Septuagint rendering and applies it to Jesus' birth: the child is Immanuel, 'God with us,' born of a virgin. Christians hold that the sign given to Ahaz carried a fuller meaning that only the birth of Christ unpacked.

Summary: 'Behold, thy King cometh unto thee... lowly, and riding upon an ass' — the king of peace, arriving without war-horse or chariot.
JewishBackground: Zechariah pictures a king who comes in humility, and the next verse banishes the battle bow and speaks peace to the nations. Rabbinic tradition includes a messianic reading of this king, though the passage's peaceful character sat uneasily beside hopes for a warrior who would throw off foreign rule. The donkey, not the war-horse, is the point: this king conquers by peace.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that Jesus staged this prophecy deliberately on Palm Sunday, entering Jerusalem on a donkey while the crowds cried for salvation. The crowd wanted the warrior; the king who came was the humble one Zechariah described, and his peace would come through the cross later that week.

Summary: 'Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD' — the last word of the Old Testament prophets.
JewishBackground: Malachi closes the prophetic books with a promise: Elijah will return before the day of the Lord, turning the hearts of fathers to children. Jewish expectation kept Elijah alive in the tradition — a cup is poured for him at the Passover Seder, and he is expected to resolve hard questions and herald the Messiah. Elijah never died, so his return seemed fitting for a herald's role.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that John the Baptist came in the spirit and power of Elijah, as Gabriel announced before his birth, and that Jesus identified John as the Elijah who was to come. The Gospels hold the tension honestly: John himself said he was not Elijah, yet Jesus said the prophecy was fulfilled in his ministry of calling Israel to repentance.

Summary: 'I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah... I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.'
JewishBackground: Jeremiah spoke to a people in exile whose covenant lay broken. His promise was of a covenant unlike the one broken at Sinai: the law internalised, sins remembered no more, all knowing the Lord. Rabbinic tradition has debated whether this is a renewal of the old covenant or something new, and most readings place its fulfilment in the messianic age to come. The promise is addressed to Israel and Judah together, a reunited people.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that Jesus inaugurated this covenant at the Last Supper — 'this cup is the new testament in my blood' — and that Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31 at length to show the old covenant giving way to the new. The law written on hearts is the Spirit's work in believers, and the forgiveness promised is the cross's work.

Summary: The Aramaic Targums — paraphrases of Scripture read in the synagogue — often make the Messiah explicit where the Hebrew text leaves him unnamed.
JewishBackground: When Hebrew ceased to be the people's everyday tongue, the Targums (Onkelos on the Torah, Jonathan on the Prophets) rendered Scripture into Aramaic, weaving explanation into the text. In messianic passages they frequently name the Messiah outright: Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 11 reads the Branch as the Messiah, and Targum Onkelos on Genesis 49 reads 'until Shiloh come' as 'until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs.' These paraphrases reached final form later than the biblical text, but the traditions they carry are ancient, and they show how Jewish hearers already heard these passages messianically.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that the Targums are valuable witnesses: the New Testament's messianic claims did not appear in a vacuum but landed among readers who already heard Messiah in these texts. Where the Hebrew is ambiguous, the Targums show one faithful Jewish way of hearing it — the way the apostles' claims echo.

Summary: The Dead Sea Scrolls community expected not one Messiah but two: a Messiah of Aaron, a priest, and a Messiah of Israel, a king — with a prophet like Moses alongside them.
JewishBackground: The Community Rule and the Testimonia scroll describe a community waiting for two anointed figures: one priestly, from Aaron's line, and one royal, from Israel, until 'the prophet and the Messiahs of Aaron and Israel' come. This was that community's expectation, shaped by its priestly character and its quarrel with the Jerusalem Temple establishment; it was not the expectation of all Jews. The two figures divide the roles that Israel's history had kept apart: priest and king.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that Jesus unites what Qumran kept apart: priest and king in one person, after the order of Melchizedek, who was both. Where Qumran waited for two messiahs, Christians hold that one Messiah fulfils both offices, and that the prophet like Moses is the same Jesus.

Summary: The Babylonian Talmud pictures mourning for 'Messiah ben Joseph who was slain' — a tradition that wrestles with a Messiah who dies before the final victory.
JewishBackground: In Sukkah 52a, the rabbis read Zechariah 12:10 — 'they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn' — of Messiah ben Joseph, slain in the wars that precede redemption. The passage is late (Talmudic period) and its interpretation is debated even within the tradition, and it is presented here as tradition, not as early proof of anything. What it shows is that Judaism itself wrestled with the figure of a slain messiah, not only with a victorious one.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that this tradition, however late, preserves the pattern the Gospels proclaim: a Messiah pierced and mourned, then vindicated. Christians hold that ben Joseph and ben David are not two figures but one Messiah, slain at his first coming and returning in glory at his second.

Summary: Seventy weeks of years decreed for Israel — a timetable ending with an anointed one cut off, one of the most debated passages in Scripture.
JewishBackground: Daniel 9 promises that seventy 'weeks' (weeks of years) will run from the decree to rebuild Jerusalem until the finishing of transgression and the anointing of the most holy. Jewish readings differ sharply on the details: the 'anointed one' cut off has been identified with various figures across the centuries, and the final week is read in several ways. The passage's difficulty is stated plainly here — confident timetables built on it should be treated with caution.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that many Christian interpreters see the seventy weeks pointing to Jesus: the anointed one cut off after sixty-nine weeks, in the fullness of time, with the final week still debated among Christians themselves. The passage is presented as a genuine messianic pointer whose details Christians continue to discuss, not as a settled calculation.

Summary: The first promise after the fall: enmity between the serpent and the woman's seed, who will bruise the serpent's head.
JewishBackground: Genesis 3:15, spoken to the serpent, promises ongoing enmity between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed, with a decisive head-wound to come. Mainstream Jewish reading centers on the human struggle with evil, while later Targumic tradition gives the verse a messianic coloring, looking to a coming deliverer. The verse is brief and its fuller meaning unfolds only across the rest of Scripture, which is why it is called the first gospel promise rather than a full one.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that the seed of the woman is Christ, born of a woman, who crushed the serpent's head at the cross — the wound to his heel being the crucifixion itself. Paul's promise that God will bruise Satan under the church's feet and Revelation's woman and dragon carry the same thread to its end.

Summary: 'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.'
JewishBackground: In Jacob's blessing on Judah, the promise of enduring kingship runs 'until Shiloh come.' Targum Onkelos renders the verse explicitly: 'until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs.' Rabbinic tradition has largely read Shiloh messianically, whatever the word's exact etymology (a place, a title, or 'the one to whom it belongs'). The verse ties the Messiah to Judah's line, not to any other tribe.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that the sceptre stayed with Judah until Jesus, of Judah's tribe, came as the one to whom the peoples gather. Hebrews notes that our Lord sprang from Judah, and Revelation names him the Lion of the tribe of Judah — the gathering of the nations to Shiloh fulfilled in the church drawn from every people.

Summary: Passover looks forward as well as back: the Seder's cup for Elijah and the cry 'Next year in Jerusalem' carry a hope that final redemption will come at Passover as the first did.
JewishBackground: The Passover story ends with a future tense: the meal remembers the Exodus and anticipates the redemption to come. A fifth cup is poured for Elijah, the herald of the Messiah, and the Seder closes with the hope of Jerusalem rebuilt. Tradition holds that the final redemption, like the first, will arrive at Passover time. This entry is the future-hope thread of Passover; the sacrifice itself is covered in The Passover Lamb and the meal's order in Passover Seder.
PointsToChrist: The site's reading is that Jesus took this forward-looking meal and filled it: at the Last Supper he spoke of eating it anew in the kingdom of God, and the church still waits at the table for the marriage supper of the Lamb. The hope Passover rehearses every year is, for Christians, already begun and not yet finished.
